definition: The war on drugs refers to the effort by the United States federal and state governments to stop the use of illegal drugs by creating new drug laws and increasing enforcement. The movement first gained prominence in the early 1970s, largely spearheaded by President Richard Nixon. The term “war on drugs” was coined by President Nixon, who declared drugs to be “public enemy number one.” See: The American Archive on Public Broadcasting. Within the framework of the war on drugs, a new federal agency, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), was created in 1973. The agency was tasked with enforcing drug laws, such as the then newly passed Controlled Substances Act. While drug laws existed before the 1970s, these laws were massively expanded under the war on drugs initiative. Many mandatory minimum sentences were instituted for drug offenses as a component of the more aggressive stance towards drug enforcement. The Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986 was instrumental in introducing mandatory minimum sentences for drug possession. As a result of the increased enforcement and mandatory minimum sentences, incarceration rates increased massively throughout the country. The United States soon became the country with the highest incarceration rate in the world. See: National Prisoner Statistics (NPS) Series, and The Federal Judicial Center - Judiciaries Worldwide. Some critics say the war on drugs began in large part to target and criminalize minorities. One rationale for this critique is the structural inequalities inherent in the framing of the laws passed at the time. For example, crack cocaine (which was more prevalent in minority communities than its powdered counterpart, cocaine), required 100 times less to be present for someone to receive the mandatory minimum sentence. Notably, the Fair Sentencing Act of 2010 lowered this ratio from 100:1 to 18:1.
